title: Potato chips in sugar water: an osmosis experiment
examples: How do you do the potato osmosis experiment?
Why does potato lose mass in sugar solution?
How do you find the concentration of potato cells?

explain.say: Here is a real experiment you can do: cut equal chips of potato, weigh each one, and drop them into cups of sugar water, from plain water to very sweet. After a day, you weigh them again.

draw.text: Potato chips in sugar water: an osmosis experiment

explain.say: Look at the left end of the line. In plain water the chip gets heavier, because water moves into the potato cells by osmosis. What do you think the chip feels like now: firm or floppy?

Now follow the line down to where it crosses zero. Here the chip neither gains nor loses mass. The sugar water matches the inside of the cells, which is called isotonic. Why would water stop moving overall?
See the right end? In strong sugar water the chip gets lighter and bendy, because water leaves its cells by osmosis. Can you say which side is more concentrated now?

Scientists plot percentage change in mass, so chips of different sizes can be compared fairly. Well done, young scientist! Challenge: read where the line crosses zero, and you have measured how sugary potato cells are.

faq.q: Why does potato gain mass in pure water?
faq.a: The potato cells are more concentrated than pure water, so water moves into them by osmosis and the chip gets heavier and firmer.
Isotonic means two solutions have the same concentration of water. Water moves both ways equally, so there is no overall change in mass.
asks: What happens where the line crosses zero?

faq.q: Why does potato lose mass in strong sugar solution?
faq.a: The sugar solution is more concentrated than the cell sap, so water moves out of the cells by osmosis and the chip loses mass and goes soft.

faq.q: Why use percentage change in mass?
faq.a: The chips may not start at exactly the same mass. Percentage change lets you compare them fairly: change divided by starting mass, times 100.
asks: How do you calculate percentage change?

faq.q: Why blot the chips before weighing?
faq.a: Water stuck on the outside would add mass that never went into the cells. Gently blotting each chip dry the same way makes the results fairer.
asks: How do you make the experiment fair?

facts: Percentage change in mass = (final mass − starting mass) ÷ starting mass × 100.
Where the graph crosses zero change, the solution has about the same water concentration as the potato cells.
